claims.text: Parents Seymour and Paula (Stolofsky) Epstein, both children of European immigrants; much of their extended families died in the Holocaust. Seymour worked for his father's house-wrecking company, then the New York City Parks Department. Records place the family in Sea Gate, a private gated community at the west end of Coney Island; Epstein described himself as growing up in Coney Island. Brother Mark; both boys gifted in maths; Jeffrey learned piano; friends called him 'Eppy'. Lafayette High School in Gravesend. Sources: Patterson/Connolly/Malloy 'Filthy Rich', a childhood friend, a classmate, public records.

Mark Epstein: real estate business; Les Wexner sold 301 East 66th Street to Mark in the early 1990s (WSJ citing Crain's); Mark told Crain's a tip from Jeffrey prompted the purchase; buyer was Ossa Properties, a former affiliate of J. Epstein & Co., Mark once listed as its president; Jeffrey's townhouse-owning entity used a unit there as its mailing address; Miami Herald reported victims housed there at $1,000 a month via Jean-Luc Brunel; Mark to WSJ: 'the only other relationship between Jeffrey and I is as landlord/tenant'; offered a Florida condo (~$100,000) for Jeffrey's 2019 bail.

claims.text: NYT: hired at Dalton in his early 20s with no college degree; yearbooks show him as a teacher from the 1974–75 year (a New York magazine profile said 1973). Eight former students said his conduct with teenage girls left a lasting impression; one recalled him as the only teacher at a party where students drank; others (e.g. Leslie Kitziger) recalled him as professional; none of the women who spoke recalled unwanted physical contact. Dismissed for poor performance; Peter Branch: 'a young teacher who didn't come up to snuff', did not recall conduct concerns being raised; Dalton did not comment.
Vanity Fair 2003: taught physics and maths at Dalton in his early 20s and tutored Ace Greenberg's son there.

Business Insider 2025: Greenberg hired him in 1976 from Dalton after a Dalton parent called; initially hired to trade options on the American Stock Exchange floor; moved to tax work for wealthy clients; limited partner 1980; Greenberg became CEO about 1978.

claims.text: Vanity Fair 2003 (citing his SEC testimony and a 1989 deposition): resigned 12 March 1981; gave SEC testimony 1 April 1981 in its inquiry into insider trading around Seagram's 1981 tender offer for St. Joe Minerals, denying knowledge of insider information involving James Cayne; SEC never charged anyone at Bear Stearns over St. Joe. He told the SEC management found 'offensive' a loan to a friend that may have been a 'Reg D' violation; in a 1989 deposition named the friend as Warren Eisenstein and the loan as about $20,000; executive committee fined him $2,500; firm still agreed to pay his bonus (expected ~$100,000). Cayne: left 'of his own volition'; Epstein denied rumours of a 'technical infringement'; Greenberg could not recall.

Business Insider 2025: Greenberg's widow recalled Greenberg getting a call that Epstein would be 'fired', reason unknown. 2003 birthday-book letters from Greenberg, Cayne (CEO from 1993), Elliot Wolk (ran an account for Robert Maxwell), Ira Zicherman (later an original trustee of Epstein's foundation), Ted Serure.

entries.topic: The missing years, the passport and Towers

claims.text: Vanity Fair 2003: some friends recall him calling himself a 'bounty hunter' recovering money for governments or the rich. Hoffenberg hired him as a consultant at $25,000 a month (per sources); office in the Villard Houses in 1987; Hoffenberg says Douglas Leese introduced them, Epstein says John Mitchell did; Towers' financial statements show a $400,000 loan to Epstein, which he says he can't remember in detail; Hoffenberg says the money for the Pennwalt bid came from him as a loan, Epstein said in 1989 he put in $300,000 of his own.

Austrian passport with his photo and another name, found in a locked safe with cash and diamonds in the July 2019 search; prosecutors' letter to Judge Berman: entry stamps for France, Spain, the UK and Saudi Arabia in the 1980s; defence: expired 32 years earlier, obtained in the 1980s for protection on Middle East travel; prosecutors noted no explanation of how he got it.

Towers: SEC charged in Feb 1993 that it reported $13m profit for four years to June 1991 while losing $137m; Hoffenberg pleaded guilty to five counts in April 1995 (about $460–462m from thousands of investors); sentenced March 1997 by Judge Robert W. Sweet to 20 years; released 2013 after 18. Hoffenberg called Epstein his 'uncharged co-conspirator' (2019). Epstein never charged.

Hoffenberg found dead in Derby, Connecticut, 23 Aug 2022, at least seven days after death; identity confirmed by dental records 26 Aug; autopsy showed no trauma, no forced entry; cause pending toxicology. In 1993 he briefly ran the New York Post. He called Epstein the scheme's architect and 'the smartest person he knew' about money.

entries.topic: Wexner, the power of attorney and the properties

claims.text: NYT 2019: Robert Meister, an insurance executive, introduced Wexner and Epstein in the mid-to-late 1980s; Epstein oversaw construction of Wexner's 316-foot yacht Limitless; July 1991 a three-page power of attorney let him hire people, sign cheques, buy and sell property and borrow money for Wexner, lasting about 16 years; 1992 New Albany, Ohio mansion bought for $3.5m (Wexner legally controlled it), bought back by a Wexner-linked entity in 1998 for $8m; 1998 Epstein took sole possession of the East 71st Street mansion (a person close to Wexner's finances says he paid $20m; no public record confirms); about 2000 an Epstein business got a Boeing 727 formerly owned by The Limited (said $10m; no public record); mid-1990s two senior L Brands executives learned he was trying to recruit Victoria's Secret models and Wexner was told; Wexner foundations gave about $21m to Epstein's charity COUQ; assets obtained worth roughly $100m in total; ties cut about 18 months after the 2006 Florida charges; July 2019 Wexner to employees: 'NEVER aware of the illegal activity'.

Business Insider 2019 (ACRIS deed records): Wexner bought 9 East 71st Street in 1989 for $13.2m; Epstein moved in 1996 (Vanity Fair); 1998 sold to Nine East 71st Street Corporation for an undisclosed amount; 2011 transferred to Maple Inc. (USVI, Epstein-controlled) for $0, Epstein signing for both sides; court document estimated value $77m.

Vanity Fair 2003: Epstein's own accounts of meeting Wexner changed (1986 in Palm Beach vs. working for him from 1989); a source close to Wexner said he gave Epstein 'the power of fiduciary over all of his private trusts and foundations'; Wexner called him 'always a most loyal friend'.

CNBC 2019: Wexner letter to his foundation said Epstein 'misappropriated vast sums of money from me and my family'; by early fall 2007 Epstein agreed to step back; he returned $46m in Apple stock and other assets to the family's YLK Charitable Fund shortly before jail in 2008; Wexner gave federal prosecutors documents.
358 El Brillo Way, Palm Beach, bought 1990 for $2.5m; sold by the estate for $18.5m; demolished from April 2021.

claims.text: 30 Jan 2026: DOJ released more than 3 million further pages, 2,000+ videos, 180,000 images; almost 3.5 million pages in total under the Act out of 6 million reviewed; deadline was 19 Dec 2025 and was missed; DOJ letter calls it compliance; critics say over-redaction and privileges the law did not allow.

Maxwell convicted December 2021 on five counts including sex trafficking; sentenced 28 June 2022 by Judge Alison Nathan to 20 years and a $750,000 fine; judge called the conduct 'heinous and predatory' and noted no acceptance of responsibility.
